title: The smaller footprint
hookLine: a good tracker doesn't conclude from a small footprint; the gradual training

cards: A wanderer named Pilotika is walking back from a visit to the Buddha, full of admiration. The brahmin Janussoni stops him and asks why he's so sure the Buddha is the real thing.

Pilotika says: I'm like an elephant tracker who sees a huge footprint and knows, that's a great bull elephant. I've seen four footprints of this man, and I'm sure. The brahmin carries the story to the Buddha.
And the Buddha, of all people, says: not so fast.

teach.b: The shorter discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint, the twenty-seventh of the Middle-Length Sayings, finishes Pilotika's picture properly.

teach.h: A BIG PRINT COULD BE A SMALLER ELEPHANT
teach.b: A skilled tracker enters an elephant forest and sees a big footprint, long and broad. He doesn't conclude: there are female dwarf elephants with big feet. Then a big footprint, and high marks where the bark is scraped.
Still not: tall female elephants could make those. Then tusk marks high on the trees. Still not: tall females with tusks could make those.
Only when he sees broken branches too, and then the bull elephant itself, under a tree or in the open, does he say: this is the great one.

teach.h: THE GRADUAL TRAINING, STEP BY STEP
teach.b: Then the Buddha lays out the gradual training. Someone hears the teaching, gains trust, and goes forth. They keep the precepts, guard the senses, stay mindful in everything they do, and find a quiet place to sit.
The hindrances fall away. They enter the first absorption, then the second, the third, the fourth. Each of these, the Buddha says, is a footprint, and a noble disciple doesn't conclude yet.
Then come deep knowledges, and still not.

teach.h: ONLY THE ELEPHANT ITSELF SETTLES IT
teach.b: Only at the end, when the mind is freed and they know it's freed, do they say: the teacher is truly awakened, and the teaching is well proclaimed. It's a caution aimed at praise of the teacher himself.
A good feeling in meditation is a footprint, not the elephant.

how: Theravada teachers present MN 27 as a model of the gradual training, from hearing the teaching and keeping precepts to meditation and liberation, and use the tracker's patience to caution students against mistaking early meditative experiences for the goal.

o: a footprint: a sign, not yet the elephant
the slow, heavy walk of a meditating monk
a sacred mark the Buddha left in stone

games.q: the tracker's trail — tap the pairs.
p: could be a female dwarf elephant

s: the Buddha accepted Pilotika's praise as it stood
he said the simile wasn't complete yet, and finished it properly.
in MN 27 even the four absorptions are only footprints
a noble disciple doesn't conclude from them; only liberation settles it.
a skilled tracker concludes from the biggest print
big prints can belong to smaller elephants; he waits to see the bull itself.

games.q: you're a tracker. you find a long, broad footprint and high scrape marks on the trees. what do you conclude?
o: a great bull elephant, for sure.
nothing yet: tall females can leave these too.
games.why: the Buddha's tracker keeps going past every sign until he sees the bull elephant itself, in a clearing or under a tree.

practice: Let the breath come and go, and within a few breaths the mind will offer a verdict: this is going well, or this isn't working, or I'm bad at this.
Call it a footprint and keep sitting; if another verdict arrives, call that a footprint too, because you're tracking, not deciding.

wordCard.voice: hatthipada. A big print that might belong to a smaller animal: a sign worth following, not yet a reason to conclude.

orig.note: Pali hatthipada: elephant's footprint. hatthi (elephant) + pada (foot, footprint).

carryVoice: Your line: not yet the elephant. One footprint is a sign, not a verdict. Day four hundred twenty-five.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 27, Culahatthipadopama Sutta (the shorter simile of the elephant's footprint)
